newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Hebron settlers warn of attacks against Jews.
newsitem.headline: Hebron settlers warn of attacks against Jews.

text.p: Jewish settlers in Hebron said the attack by an off-duty Israeli soldier who wounded seven Palestinians on Wednesday could have ignited a bloody reprisal if the Israeli army had not been there.

Leaders of the militant Jewish community in the heart of Hebron called on Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu not to redeploy troops from 80 percent of the town under the self-rule accord with the PLO.
"If the army here wasn't in total control of the area we would very likely have seen mass riots and mass murder against Jews," said Hebron settler leader Noam Arnon.
He was speaking after a soldier from a settlement near Jerusalem fired into the Hebron vegetable market, wounding seven Palestinians including women and youths.
Arnon condemned the attack but said settlers were endangered by the self-rule agreement that Netanyahu was poised to seal with Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
Other settlers said hundreds of Palestinians gathered at the market and were preparing to storm settlers' homes when soldiers intervened. Palestinians said they were beaten.

The army, fearing the shooting would reignite the gun batles that Israeli troops waged with Arabs in September in the Israeli-occupied territories, clamped a curfew on Palestinians in the town and placed two armoured personnel carriers on a hill overlooking Hebron.

Troops said the gunman was wearing an army uniform and the skullcap of a religious Jew. Soldiers pounced on him seconds after he began firing randomly at Palestinians. Security sources said he was from the Maaleh Adumim settlement near Jerusalem and was not stationed in Hebron.

Under the Hebron deal, Israel is due to hand over 80 percent of the town -- home to 400 Jewish settlers and 100,000 Arabs -- to Palestinian self-rule. Soldiers will remain posted in and around Jewish enclaves to protect the settlers.
Settlers fear the redeployment will leave them vulnerable in the violence-prone town and have lobbied Netanyahu -- the man they helped elect -- to call it off.

"The fact that Israel was able to impose a curfew immediately afterwards helped calm the situation. Had it not been able to do so, well you can use your imagination," said settler spokesman David Wilder.

Hebron is the only area in the West Bank where Jews settled in the heart of an Arab community and has been a flashpoint for Arab-Israeli violence. Palestinians say they are in more danger from the settlers than the other way around.
In 1994, a Jewish settler murdered 29 Palestinian worshippers at a religious site where both Jews and Moslems believe the biblical Abraham was buried.
As Israeli and Palestinian negotiators have edged closer to reaching an agreement, tension in Hebron has soared.
Twice in the last week police evicted Jewish settlers from empty Arab homes after pre-dawn raids, and petrol bombs have been thrown daily at Jewish homes in the town.
Settlers denounced the shooting on Wednesday and said it only harmed their chance of blocking an Israeli withdrawal.

"The council of settlements in Judea, Samaria (the West Bank) and Gaza condemns attacks against innocent people. Every incident of this kind only weakens the Jewish community," said the main settler umbrella group in a statement.
Parliament member Benny Elon of the right wing Moledet party described the shooting as "political stupidity."
"What do they think, that it will now be easier for Netanyahu to resist pressure to redeploy?" he said.
